revenue.tip: Total sales before any expenses. The top line.
revenue.what: How big the business is and how fast demand for its products is growing.
revenue.compare: Prior years (trend), competitors’ growth, and the overall market growth rate.
revenue.misleading: Acquisitions, currency moves or one-off contracts can inflate growth. Revenue says nothing about profit.

growth.what: The pace at which the top line is expanding.
growth.compare: Multi-year trend, peers, and whether growth is organic or bought (M&A).
growth.misleading: Easy comparisons after a bad year, price-only growth in inflation, or growth that requires huge spending.

grossProfit.what: Dollars left after paying the direct cost of delivering the product.
grossProfit.compare: Its trend vs revenue growth — gross profit should grow at least as fast.
grossProfit.misleading: Companies classify costs differently (e.g. hosting, shipping), so peer comparisons need care.

grossMargin.tip: Gross Profit / Revenue. What remains of each $1 of sales after direct costs.
grossMargin.what: How much revenue remains after direct costs — a sign of pricing power and product economics.
grossMargin.misleading: Different industries naturally have very different gross margins (software ~75%, retail ~25%).

opMargin.tip: Operating Income / Revenue. Profit from core operations per $1 of sales.
opMargin.what: How profitable the core business is after all operating costs (R&D, S&M, G&A).
opMargin.compare: Trend over time (operating leverage?), peers, and management’s long-term target.
opMargin.misleading: Heavy growth investment can depress it temporarily; one-off charges or capitalised costs can distort it.

netMargin.tip: Net Income / Revenue. Bottom-line profit per $1 of sales.
netMargin.what: The share of revenue that ends up as accounting profit for shareholders.
netMargin.compare: History and peers; and against operating margin to see the impact of interest and taxes.
netMargin.misleading: Affected by one-offs, tax benefits, interest, gains on investments — not purely operating performance.

fcf.tip: Operating Cash Flow − CapEx. Cash the business actually generates.
fcf.what: Cash that could be returned to owners, used to pay debt, or reinvested.
fcf.compare: Net income (cash conversion), prior years, and FCF per share over time.
fcf.misleading: Ignoring stock-based compensation inflates FCF; cutting CapEx boosts FCF short term but can hurt growth.

fcfMargin.tip: FCF / Revenue. Cash generated per $1 of sales.
fcfMargin.what: How efficiently revenue converts into real cash.
fcfMargin.misleading: Working-capital swings or deferred revenue can boost one year. Low margin may reflect growth CapEx.

netCash.tip: Cash − Debt. Positive = net cash; negative = net debt.
netCash.what: Financial cushion (or burden) on the balance sheet.
netCash.compare: Annual FCF and EBITDA — how many years to pay off net debt?
netCash.misleading: Cash may be trapped abroad or needed for operations; leases and off-balance-sheet obligations are excluded.

currentRatio.tip: Current Assets / Current Liabilities. Short-term liquidity.
currentRatio.what: Whether the company can meet obligations due within a year.
currentRatio.compare: Industry norms and the company’s own history. ~1.5–2.0 is typical comfort.
currentRatio.misleading: Inventory that cannot be sold or receivables that won’t be collected inflate it. Subscription businesses often run < 1 safely (deferred revenue).

debtEbitda.tip: Total Debt / EBITDA. Years of EBITDA needed to repay debt (rough leverage).
debtEbitda.what: How leveraged the company is relative to its earnings power.
debtEbitda.compare: Industry peers, the company’s history and its debt covenants — there is no universal threshold.
debtEbitda.misleading: EBITDA ignores CapEx, interest and taxes, so leverage can be worse than it looks. Cyclical EBITDA can collapse.

nopat.tip: Operating Income × (1 − Tax Rate). Operating profit after tax, ignoring financing.
nopat.what: The after-tax profit generated by the operations, independent of how the company is financed.
nopat.compare: Invested capital (→ ROIC) and its growth over time.
nopat.misleading: Using a statutory tax rate when the real cash tax rate differs; one-off items in operating income.

investedCapital.tip: Capital tied up in operations: Equity + Debt − Cash (simplified).
investedCapital.what: How much capital the business needs to run.
investedCapital.compare: NOPAT (→ ROIC) and its growth vs revenue growth.
investedCapital.misleading: Goodwill from acquisitions, buybacks (reduce equity), and accounting choices change it a lot.

roic.tip: NOPAT / Invested Capital. Return on each $1 of capital in the business.
roic.what: How efficiently the business turns invested capital into operating profit — a key quality signal.
roic.compare: WACC (value creation if ROIC > WACC), peers, and its trend.
roic.misleading: Tiny invested capital (asset-light, negative working capital) can make ROIC look enormous; one great year isn’t durable.

wacc.tip: Weighted Average Cost of Capital — the return investors require.
wacc.what: The hurdle rate a business must beat to create value.
wacc.compare: ROIC. Typical large-cap WACC is 7–10%; riskier companies higher.
wacc.misleading: Small input changes (beta, risk premium) swing it a lot — false precision.

marketCap.tip: Share Price × Shares Outstanding. Market value of the equity.
marketCap.what: What the market currently charges for the whole company’s equity.
marketCap.compare: Earnings, FCF, and intrinsic value estimates.
marketCap.misleading: Use diluted shares; share price alone tells you nothing about cheapness.

eps.tip: Net Income / Shares Outstanding. Profit per share.
eps.compare: EPS growth over years; Diluted vs Basic.
eps.misleading: Buybacks raise EPS without business improvement; one-offs distort it; “adjusted” EPS often excludes real costs.

pe.tip: Price / EPS (= Market Cap / Net Income). $ paid per $1 of earnings.
pe.what: How much investors pay for current earnings.
pe.compare: History, peers, the market (~15–25x), and expected growth (PEG).
pe.misleading: Low P/E can be a value trap (declining business); high P/E can be cheap for fast growers. Cyclical earnings peak when P/E looks lowest.

ev.tip: Market Cap + Debt − Cash. Value of the operating business.
ev.what: The price to buy the whole business, including its debt and keeping its cash.
ev.misleading: Should include preferred stock, minority interests and leases for precision — this simplified version ignores them.

evEbitda.tip: EV / EBITDA. Valuation independent of capital structure.
evEbitda.what: Price of the whole business relative to its operating earnings before D&A.
evEbitda.compare: Peers in the same industry and historical range.
evEbitda.misleading: EBITDA ignores CapEx — capital-intensive businesses look cheaper than they are.

pfcf.tip: Market Cap / FCF. $ paid per $1 of annual free cash flow.
pfcf.what: How expensive the stock is relative to the cash it generates.
pfcf.compare: P/E (cash vs accounting), history, peers. Inverse of FCF Yield.
pfcf.misleading: One-year FCF can be lumpy; SBC is not deducted from FCF.

fcfYield.tip: FCF / Market Cap. Annual cash return per $100 of market value.
fcfYield.what: The cash “earnings yield” you get at today’s price, before growth.
fcfYield.compare: Bond yields, other stocks, and expected FCF growth.
fcfYield.misleading: High yield + shrinking FCF = trap. Low yield can be fine with high growth.

dcf.tip: Present value of future free cash flows.
dcf.what: An estimate of intrinsic value based on your assumptions about future cash flows.
dcf.misleading: Output is only as good as inputs; terminal value often is 60–80% of the value. Treat it as a range.

upside.what: How far the estimated value is from today’s price.
upside.compare: Your required margin of safety, and the bear/bull range.
upside.misleading: A precise number from imprecise inputs. Check what the current price implies instead.

ebitda.tip: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation & Amortisation.
ebitda.what: A rough proxy of operating earnings before capital structure and non-cash D&A.
ebitda.compare: Operating income and FCF — how much CapEx is it ignoring?
ebitda.misleading: EBITDA is NOT cash flow. It ignores CapEx, working capital, taxes and interest.
